how to get a coat of arms
a: The grant of arms is the formal legal process by which a coat of arms is officially awarded to an individual or organization. In England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, this is managed by the College of Arms (a royal corporation of heralds established in 1484 by King Richard III). The process begins with a petition to the Earl Marshal (the Duke of Norfolk) through one of the Kings of Arms (Garter, Clarenceux, or Norroy & Ulster), who determines if the applicant is eligible—arms are granted by the Crown's prerogative, typically to individuals who have achieved notable distinction, or to corporations, institutions, and towns. If approved, the heralds at the College design a unique coat of arms (ensuring no conflict with existing arms), and Letters Patent (the official grant document, beautifully hand-illuminated on vellum with the armorial bearings painted in full color and sealed with the seal of the relevant King of Arms) are issued, conferring the exclusive right to bear those arms. Fees for a personal grant of arms in England start at approximately £8,000 (as of the 2020s), while corporate grants are higher, reflecting the extensive research, design work, and art involved. In Scotland, the Lord Lyon King of Arms grants arms through a separate petition process, with fees structured differently and including the requirement for matriculation (registration) of arms with differences for cadet branches.

heraldic jurisdictions around the world
a: Heraldic authority is organized nationally, with different jurisdictions governing the use and granting of arms. England, Wales, and Northern Ireland fall under the College of Arms in London, led by the Earl Marshal with three Kings of Arms (Garter, Clarenceux, Norroy & Ulster), six Heralds, and four Pursuivants—the College is a corporation of 13 officers crown-appointed for life and has maintained continuous records since the 14th century. Scotland is separate under the Lord Lyon King of Arms (based in Edinburgh), a judge of the realm who sits in the Lyon Court and has both heraldic and judicial authority—Scottish heraldry differs in its regulation of clan arms, cadet branches via matriculation, and the strict prohibition on assuming arms without Lyon's permission. The Canadian Heraldic Authority (established 1988 in Ottawa) is the youngest official heraldic authority, created by the Governor General on the advice of the Queen's Privy Council, and grants arms to Canadian citizens and organizations—it pioneered the inclusion of Indigenous symbolism and modern design in official heraldry. The Office of the Chief Herald of Ireland (Genealogical Office, Dublin) grants arms under the authority of the Government of Ireland, though its legal basis differs as Ireland does not have the same Crown prerogative framework. South Africa's Bureau of Heraldry (established 1963) registers arms under the Heraldry Act. The United States has no official heraldic authority—Americans seeking arms may petition the English College of Arms (if they can prove English descent), the Scottish Lord Lyon, or the Canadian Heraldic Authority if eligible, or acquire arms from voluntary societies like the American College of Heraldry or the US Heraldic Registry, but these have no legal force.

q: What is personal heraldry?
How are family coats of arms inherited?
What are marks of cadency in heraldry?
What is the label for the eldest son?
What do crescent, mullet, martlet, annulet, fleur-de-lis, and rose mean as cadency marks?
What are differencing marks of cadency?
cadency marks label crescent mullet martlet annulet fleur-de-lis rose cross
heraldic differencing for sons
a: Personal heraldry coats of arms are inherited by descendants of the original grantee or bearer. In English heraldry, arms are inherited by all male-line descendants (primogeniture inheritance), but differencing marks of cadency (called brisures) identify the position of the bearer within the family. The standard English cadency system uses small charges placed on the shield: a label (a horizontal bar with three pendants) for the eldest son during his father's lifetime (removed upon inheritance); a crescent for the second son; a mullet (five-pointed star) for the third son; a martlet (footless bird) for the fourth; an annulet (ring) for the fifth; a fleur-de-lis for the sixth; a rose for the seventh; a cross for the eighth; and a double tressure for the ninth son. In Scottish heraldry, the cadency system is more complex: a bordure (border) with various tinctures and charges is used for differencing, and all cadets must matriculate (formally register) their version of arms with the Lord Lyon, who assigns specific differences—this results in a rich, well-documented system of Scottish family arms that are individually unique. Marks of cadency can be combined for subsequent generations: a crescent (second son) with a label (his eldest son) indicates a second son's eldest son.

a: Corporate heraldry encompasses coats of arms for universities, colleges, schools (Oxford and Cambridge colleges have some of the oldest corporate arms), hospitals, livery companies (the Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths, Mercers, etc.), commercial companies (many with modern arms including logos), and military units (regiments, ships, and air squadrons). Civic heraldry includes arms for towns, cities, counties, and states—often incorporating local symbols (the city seal or crest with a ship for a port town, wheat for an agricultural region, crossed swords for a military garrison). National coats of arms appear on passports, currency, and official documents (e.g., the Great Seal of the United States with its eagle, the Royal Arms of the United Kingdom, the French RF monogram). Ecclesiastical heraldry uses specific symbols of office: bishops place a green galero (a wide-brimmed hat with cords and tassels, 6 tassels per side) behind their shield; archbishops use 10 tassels per side with a cross; the Pope uses the crossed keys of St. Peter and the Papal tiara (or a mitre in modern Francis's arms). Cardinals display a red galero with 15 tassels per side. Dioceses and abbeys also bear arms, often combining the arms of their patron saint or founder with local symbols. Military heraldry includes regimental badges, naval ship seals (typically with an anchor, ship, or naval crown), and air force squadron crests, all following heraldic conventions adapted for military tradition and identification.

non-European heraldic traditions worldwide
a: Heraldic traditions exist in many cultures beyond the European system. Japan has mon (家紋 kamon), family crests used since the 12th century to identify aristocratic clans—these are simplified circular emblems featuring plants (paulownia, chrysanthemum, cherry blossom), animals (crane, butterfly), geometric patterns, Chinese characters, or abstract motifs, typically rendered in a single color (black, white, or red) without the tincture rules of European heraldry. Many African cultures have emblematic traditions: the Akan people of Ghana use Adinkra symbols (stamped patterns on cloth and architectural elements, each with a specific proverb or meaning—like the Gye Nyame symbolizing the supremacy of God, or Sankofa symbolizing learning from the past) though these are not strictly heraldic in the European sense. The Ashanti Golden Stool and Yoruba beaded crowns carry royal insignia functions parallel to heraldry. Native American traditions include totem poles (Pacific Northwest, showing clan lineage and history through carved animal figures), and indigenous seals used by tribal nations (the Great Seal of the Navajo Nation with its rainbow, sacred animals, and corn stalks). In the Arab world, calligraphic emblems and the use of the sword, eagle (Saladin's Eagle), and star-and-crescent appear on national emblems, with the Arabic script often serving a heraldic function. Russian heraldry follows European conventions but with distinctive features: the double-headed eagle (Byzantine tradition), city arms with elaborate decorations, and a strong tradition of municipal heraldry. Both North and South American heraldry blend European heraldic traditions with indigenous symbols—armillary spheres, llamas, condors, pumas, and native flora appear on national and civic arms throughout the Americas.
